planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in spring in free-draining, humus-rich soil in a shaded, sheltered spot; where winters are cold, grow in a container and overwinter frost-free.

directions: This scrambling perennial climbs from a fleshy underground tuber, dying back to rest after its unusual winter flowering season. Large pendulous orange bells open from autumn through winter, followed by orange fruit that tastes something like a cross between a fig and a melon and has traditionally been eaten fresh in its native Canary Islands. Give it a shaded, sheltered niche with something to scramble over, since in the wild it threads through gaps and shrubs at the edge of laurel forest. Let the soil dry out somewhat while the tuber is dormant to avoid rot.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or young container plants in spring into acidic, humus-rich, reliably moist soil in a sheltered, shaded site.

directions: Endemic to the cool, cloud-wrapped laurel forest of Madeira, this evergreen tree bears glossy leathery leaves and dangling racemes of small white, fragrant, bell-shaped flowers in autumn that closely recall lily-of-the-valley. It wants the same constantly moist, acidic, humus-rich footing it gets in its native mountain forest, along with protection from drying wind and intense sun. Because it is only marginally frost-hardy, treat it as a sheltered woodland-garden specimen in borderline climates or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover. Propagation is almost always by semi-ripe cuttings, since seed is rarely available outside its native range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded woodland edge or stream bank, sheltered from strong wind.

directions: The largest fuchsia in the world, this New Zealand forest tree sheds its thin bark in papery orange-cinnamon curls and carries drooping, dusky purple-green flowers that are unique among fuchsias in producing blue pollen. The small purple-black berries that follow, known to Maori as konini, are sweet and edible straight off the tree and were once a valued seasonal forest food. It grows best as an understory or edge-of-woodland tree with constant soil moisture and some overhead shelter, and establishes readily from cuttings taken from semi-hardwood growth.

planting.note: Establish rooted cuttings in spring at a woodland edge or against a sturdy support, since the hooked prickles need something to scramble and climb over.

directions: This wiry New Zealand bramble earned its common name from prickles so persistently hooked that getting tangled in a thicket of it was joked to be like dealing with a lawyer. It scrambles and climbs through shrubs and small trees at forest margins, bearing small lobed leaves and clusters of small orange-yellow, raspberry-like fruit that are edible and were eaten by Maori in small quantities. Grow it where its climbing habit can be put to use, such as over a stump or fence at the shaded edge of a woodland planting, and expect it to need occasional cutting back to keep it in bounds.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring in cool, humus-rich soil in dappled shade beneath taller trees or shrubs.

directions: Native to the cold Nothofagus beech forests of southern Patagonia, this dense, twiggy currant is exceptionally cold-hardy for a shrub from such a wet, maritime climate. Small tubular flowers give way to tart red-orange berries that were gathered by indigenous Patagonian peoples and are still foraged locally today. It prefers the cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil of its native forest floor and performs best tucked beneath larger shrubs or trees where it gets dappled light rather than baking sun.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets or plant container specimens in spring in sharply draining soil in a sheltered, partly shaded spot such as a rock crevice or warm wall base.

directions: Unusually hardy for a bromeliad, this Chilean native forms a dense rosette of stiff, spine-edged strap leaves that grows naturally on rocks and tree branches in coastal forest. Just before flowering, the central leaves flush bright red, setting off the small powder-blue flowers that cluster at the heart of the rosette in late summer. It wants sharp drainage around its roots but appreciates humidity and shelter overhead, making a rock garden, wall crevice, or the crook of a tree a good home. Established clumps slowly produce offsets that can be detached and replanted.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade, echoing its native laurel-forest understory.

directions: A slow-growing evergreen tree of the Canarian and Madeiran laurisilva, Mocán bears small white-to-pink bell flowers followed by soft, mucilaginous berries that ripen from red to black. The berries have long been fermented into a traditional sweet syrup or liqueur known as mocanera in the Canary Islands. It needs the cool, humid, sheltered conditions of a laurel-forest understory to thrive, with steady moisture and protection from drying wind and harsh midday sun. Outside its native climate it is best suited to a sheltered woodland-garden niche in mild, frost-free regions.
sources: Jardín Botánico Canario Viera y Clavijo

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded or lightly dappled site, protected from strong wind while young.

directions: This dense-canopied evergreen is one of the characteristic large trees of the ancient laurisilva forest of the Canary Islands and Madeira, with dark, glossy, laurel-like leaves and small inconspicuous greenish flowers. Historically its strong, fine-grained timber was prized for furniture and construction on the islands. As a true forest-canopy and understory species it tolerates deep shade well, especially while young, and prefers the cool, constantly humid conditions of a cloud-forest climate rather than hot, dry sun.
sources: Jardín Botánico Canario Viera y Clavijo

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing room for a broad eventual canopy.

directions: A relative of the cultivated olive, this Macaronesian laurel-forest tree carries small, leathery, pale-veined leaves and inconspicuous flowers followed by small dark drupes that are not grown as food. Its pale, dense wood gave rise to the Portuguese name pau branco, or white wood, and it has long been valued as a durable timber tree on Madeira and the Canary Islands. In the garden it is a slow but sturdy shade or woodland-edge tree for mild, humid climates, tolerating partial shade well once established.
sources: Jardín Botánico Canario Viera y Clavijo

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, with shelter from strong wind while establishing.

directions: A large relative of the cultivated avocado, this evergreen laurel-forest tree of Madeira and the Canary Islands has long been prized for its rich reddish timber, historically used in fine furniture and shipbuilding and giving it the common name Madeira mahogany. It carries glossy dark leaves and small, inconspicuous yellow-green flowers, with fruit that is not cultivated for eating. In cultivation it prefers the same cool, humid, sheltered woodland conditions it gets in its native cloud-forest range, growing well as a shade or partial-shade specimen tree in mild, frost-free gardens.
sources: Jardín Botânico Canario Viera y Clavijo

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in any reasonably drained soil; trim to shape as a hedge or let it grow as a loose shade shrub.

directions: This tough New Zealand native carries glossy, bright apple-green, rounded leaves on a dense evergreen shrub that is as happy forming a wind-shorn hedge on an exposed coast as it is filling in a partly shaded woodland planting. Small greenish flowers are followed by small dark fruit on female plants where a male is nearby for pollination. It tolerates wide swings of light from full coastal sun to woodland shade, along with salt spray and wind, making it an unusually adaptable evergreen screen or filler shrub. Propagate from semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in partial shade; little supplemental care is needed once established.

directions: Despite the common name, this dense, twiggy dioecious shrub is native across the mountains of Africa and Asia rather than being a true boxwood, and it is grown for its tiny glossy leaves tinged bronze-red when new. Inconspicuous flowers on female plants mature into small blue-purple berries if a male shrub is growing nearby. It is slow growing and undemanding, tolerating heat, drought, and partial shade equally well once rooted in, which makes it a popular low-water filler or informal low hedge in mild-winter gardens.

planting.note: Plant young container trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade, where the striking juvenile foliage form is best appreciated.

directions: One of New Zealand's most distinctive forest trees, the lancewood spends its first fifteen to twenty years in a bizarre juvenile form: a single rigid, unbranched stem bearing stiff, narrow, sharply toothed leaves angled sharply downward. Botanists believe this odd juvenile shape evolved to discourage browsing by the now-extinct giant moa. Eventually the tree transforms abruptly into a very different, broad-leaved, branching adult canopy form. Grow it in a shaded or partly shaded woodland setting while young, where the architectural juvenile stage makes a striking accent, and be patient with its slow early growth.
